newsitem.title: FINLAND: Summit tough to predict as Russia raises stakes.
newsitem.headline: Summit tough to predict as Russia raises stakes.

text.p: By Nicholas Doughty, Diplomatic Correspondent
In the face of a determined assault from Moscow on NATO plans for enlargement, the U.S.-Russian summit may be far from the harmonious and well-orchestrated event it was meant to be.

Russia seems determined to prove a point by turning up the anti-NATO rhetoric before President Boris Yeltsin and President Bill Clinton start their meeting over dinner in the Finnish capital later on Thursday.
The United States has been trying to smooth the waters, stressing others areas where progress is possible, such as Russia's economic reforms.
It may all be rhetorical bluster, part of the usual diplomatic poker game that always precedes such occasions.
But Yeltsin must be careful to show his communist and nationalist critics at home that he is firmly in charge after months of illness -- and that he is fighting Russia's corner.
His spokesman, Sergei Yastrzhembsky, gave some of the flavour of this on the eve of the summit.

"President Yeltsin and the Russian leadership are convinced that NATO's plans to expand to the east, if realised, could be the West's biggest strategic mistake since the end of the Cold War," he told reporters.

His comments raised the possibility that Yeltsin could repeat his performance at a 1994 European security summit in Budapest, where he publicly attacked Clinton and said NATO risked plunging the continent into a "cold peace".
Since then, the West has done its best to reassure Russia that NATO enlargement will not present any kind of threat, offering Moscow a new relationship and arms control concessions.
But diplomats say Yeltsin has no need to give ground in Helsinki and may hold out for a better deal.
NATO will not invite new members to start talks until a summit in July and they will not actually join before 1999.
Yeltsin will also have a keen eye on the Duma, the Russian parliament which is dominated by his fiercest critics. The Duma was to debate an anti-NATO resolution on Thursday.
As a result, he may be prepared to push very hard in Helsinki or even leave without any kind of agreement.
Summits are normally orderly affairs, planned and orchestrated in fine detail and that is certainly the preferred option for Washington.
U.S. officials have been carefully shifting the focus away from hopes of major progress on the NATO issue, towards other questions such as nuclear disarmament and economic affairs.
The United States, famous for its mastery of public relations and image, may find it has a tough job on its hands.

Clinton is in a wheelchair after injuring his leg in a freak accident last week. Yeltsin, by contrast, appears to be in robust health after his long illness and has just completed a far-reaching cabinet reshuffle to show he is in charge.
This time, too, the Russians seem to have a well-oiled publicity machine, throwing off the Soviet-style image and matching the best "spin doctors" Washington has to offer.
Yeltsin's spokesman came to Helsinki a day early to lay down Moscow's line on NATO, accompanied by other Russian officials who have been briefing reporters with a new-found confidence.
On Wednesday, U.S. briefers were nowhere to be found in Helsinki.
